title: Coasts 1: Waves and Coastal Processes
subject: Geography
description: Wave terms, constructive and destructive waves, marine erosion, weathering, transport, longshore drift, deposition and wave refraction.
author: Erick

cards.back: The area where the land meets the sea.

cards.front: Give reasons why we need to know about the coast (UK / Isle of Man).
cards.back: We live on an island surrounded by water, many people depend on the coast for work, sea levels are rising, and tides affect sailing times.

cards.front: Beach profile made by constructive waves
cards.back: Gentle (shallow) and wide, with ridges of material (berms) built up at the top of the beach.

cards.front: Beach profile made by destructive waves
cards.back: Steep and narrow, because the strong backwash drags material back out to sea.
Destructive waves are taller and have more energy. Constructive waves have a longer wavelength. Constructive waves add material; destructive waves remove it.

cards.front: List three factors that affect the type of wave that arrives at the coast.
cards.back: Length of the fetch / strength of the wind / steepness of the beach

cards.front: How does the fetch affect a wave?
cards.back: The longer the fetch, the stronger the wave.

cards.front: How does wind strength affect a wave?
cards.back: The stronger the wind, the more energy the waves have.

cards.front: How does a steep beach affect waves?
cards.back: A steeper beach makes waves more destructive.

cards.front: Why does a cliff made of soluble material erode faster?
cards.back: It is broken down chemically by corrosion (solution), so it is eroded much more rapidly.
Weathering of the cliff from above, e.g. rain, surface run-off and freeze-thaw.

The prevailing wind makes waves hit the coast at an angle. The swash carries material up the beach at that angle. The backwash returns it straight down (perpendicular) under gravity. This repeats in a zig-zag, moving material along the beach.

When waves lose energy and can no longer carry material, e.g. in sheltered bays, where the fetch is short, or where constructive waves dominate.
Waves slow down in shallower water near headlands and bend. This concentrates wave energy on the headlands and spreads it out in the bays.

questions.question: Which is the distance the wind blows over the water?
questions.explanation: Fetch is the distance the wind blows over the water. A longer fetch gives a stronger wave.

questions.question: Which describes a constructive wave?
questions.explanation: Constructive waves have a strong swash, weak backwash, low height and long wavelength, and they add material.

questions.question: Rocks carried by a wave being thrown against the coast is called...
questions.explanation: Abrasion is rocks thrown against the coast. Attrition is rocks in the wave crashing into each other.

questions.question: Which type of transport is the bouncing of material?
questions.explanation: Saltation is bouncing. Traction is rolling or dragging, suspension is carrying, solution is dissolving.

questions.question: In longshore drift, how does the backwash move?
options: At an angle, pushed by the wind
Along the beach parallel to the shore
Straight down the beach under gravity
Up the beach at an angle
questions.explanation: The swash goes up at an angle with the prevailing wind; the backwash returns perpendicular to the shore under gravity.

questions.question: Which makes waves more destructive?
questions.explanation: A steeper beach makes waves more destructive. A longer fetch and stronger wind also make stronger waves.
